Mount Everest.text: Surveyors got exactly 29,000 ft, but announced 29,002 so it wouldn't look like a rounded guess.
Mount Everest.evidence: Peak XV (measured in feet) was calculated to be exactly 29,000 ft (8,839.2 m) high, but was publicly declared to be 29,002 ft (8,839.8 m) in order to avoid the impression that an exact height of 29000 ft was nothing more than a rounded estimate.

K2.text: Aleister Crowley was part of the first serious attempt to climb it, in 1902.
K2.evidence: The first serious attempt to climb K2 was undertaken in 1902 by Oscar Eckenstein, Aleister Crowley, Jules Jacot-Guillarmod, Heinrich Pfannl, Victor Wessely, and Guy Knowles via the Northeast Ridge.

Kangchenjunga.text: In 1962 a lama led over 300 followers up its snow slopes to open the way to a legendary valley of immortality.
Kangchenjunga.evidence: For generations, there have been legends recounted by the inhabitants of the areas surrounding Kanchenjunga, both in Sikkim and in Nepal, that there is a valley of immortality hidden on its slopes. ... In Tibetan, this valley is known as Beyul Demoshong. In 1962, a Tibetan Lama by the name of Tulshuk Lingpa led over 300 followers into the high snow slopes of Kanchenjunga, to "open the way" to Beyul Demoshong.

Lhotse.text: Its middle summit was the highest unclimbed named point on Earth until a Russian team reached it in 2001.
Lhotse.evidence: Lhotse Middle remained, for a long time, the highest unclimbed named point on Earth; its first ascent was made on 23 May 2001 by Eugeny Vinogradsky, Sergei Timofeev, Alexei Bolotov and Petr Kuznetsov of a Russian expedition.

Makalu.text: The area around it has been a focus for yeti expeditions.
Makalu.evidence: The Makalu area has been a focus for yeti expeditions.

Cho Oyu.text: In 2017 Valery Rozov BASE jumped off it from 7,700 metres.
Cho Oyu.evidence: Valery Rozov BASE jumped off Cho Oyu in 2017 from 7,700 metres (25,250 ft)

Dhaulagiri I.text: Its 1960 first ascent used a plane that set the record for highest fixed-wing landing, then crashed and was abandoned.
Dhaulagiri I.evidence: Swiss-Austrian expedition led by Max Eiselin makes the first successful ascent to the summit of Dhaulagiri. ... First Himalayan climb supported by the first prototype fixed-wing aircraft, which, after establishing the still standing record for highest fixed wing landing, eventually crashed in Hidden Valley north of the mountain during takeoff and was abandoned.

Manaslu.text: A 2021 investigation found most climbers who claimed to have summited it never stood on the true peak.
Manaslu.evidence: Like Shishapangma, Manaslu has a false summit that is separated from the true summit by a long and dangerous sharp corniced ridge. In 2021, an investigation by a team of international experts reported in the American Alpine Journal that most climbers who claimed to have summited Manaslu had not, in fact, stood on the true peak.

Nanga Parbat.text: Hermann Buhl finished the first ascent alone on a methamphetamine-based drug, then spent the night standing on a ledge.
Nanga Parbat.evidence: Nanga Parbat was first climbed, via the Rakhiot Flank (East Ridge), on July 3, 1953, by Austrian climber Hermann Buhl on the German–Austrian Nanga Parbat expedition, a member of a German-Austrian team. ... The final push for the summit was dramatic: Buhl continued alone for the final 1,300 metres (4,300 ft), after his companions had turned back. Under the influence of the drug pervitin (based on the stimulant methamphetamine used by soldiers during World War II), padutin, and tea from coca leaves, he reached the summit dangerously late, at 7:00 p.m., the climbing harder and more time-consuming than he had anticipated. ... Caught by darkness, he was forced to bivouac standing upright on a narrow ledge, holding a small handhold with one hand.

Annapurna I.text: It is named after the Hindu goddess of food, and its name can be translated as "everlasting food".
Annapurna I.evidence: The mountain is named after Annapurna, the Hindu goddess of food and nourishment, who is said to reside there. The name Annapurna is derived from the Sanskrit-language words purna ("filled") and anna ("food"), and can be translated as "everlasting food".
